newsitem.title: CHINA: World handover celebrations tempered by fears.
newsitem.headline: World handover celebrations tempered by fears.

text.p: Ethnic Chinese around the world on Tuesday celebrated Hong Kong's return to China, but the excitement for many was tempered by concerns for human rights under Beijing's rule.
Britain's Prince Charles handed back Hong Kong to China at midnight on Monday after more than 150 years of colonial rule.
Thousands gathered to mark the event in Chinese communities from Calcutta to New York, feasting and making merry at huge parties and colourful parades.

"This is a glorious day for us, especially since it's a peaceful day," said Yi Lum, organiser of a parade in Chinatown in New York City. "We feel very proud that Hong Kong is being returned to China. We see a very bright future."
In the eastern Indian city of Calcutta more than 2,000 ethnic Chinese gathered at a school compound to drink, sing and dance over the event.
They watched the proceedings live on television and shouted in joy when the Chinese flag was hoisted.
Celebrations in Vancouver, Canada, which has seen a dramatic influx of immigrants from Hong Kong in recent years, included an early morning party at a classical garden.

In London, thousands gathered in the London Arena, a venue usually used for concerts and boxing matches but which had been decorated to resemble Hong Kong's famous Temple Street, hung with red lanterns and fairy lights.
While most were happy to see the end to colonial rule in Hong Kong and the return of the territory of 6.4 million people to the Chinese motherland, many also feared for the future of human rights.
Dissident Lian Shengde, a leader of the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy protests brutally crushed in June 1989, now living in the United States, said there was no reason to celebrate.
"July 1 is a very sad day. This is not about China getting back land they once had. It's about totalitarianism spreading into a free, democratic and prosperous region," Lian said.
Demonstrators in Canada scheduled pro-democracy protests outside Chinese diplomatic posts in Vancouver, Toronto and Ottawa.

"With the largest Hong Kong immigrant population in the world, the Chinese communities in Canada are visibly concerned about the loss of civil liberties after the handover," said Henry Chau, head of the Vancouver Society in Support of Democratic Movement.

The Beijing-appointed provisional legislature sworn in soon after the handover, replacing a partially-elected chamber, passed a bill to curb relatively modest recent political reforms as its first order of business early on Tuesday.
International human rights group Amnesty International said the new legislature's moves had ruined what could have been a wonderful day.

"It's a shame that ordinary Hong Kong people celebrate their freedoms in such a peaceful way and that their new unelected legislature that will be sitting tonight will be curbing those freedoms," the group's asia director Rory Mungoven told Reuters.

There was little obvious emotion over the event in London, but Bermudans gathered around television sets to watch it live in the knowledge that their island was now Britain's most populous and prosperous overseas possession.
"There's a serious awareness that Bermuda is now the biggest and most prosperous part of what's left of the empire," said one resident.
